clue.text: Unnecessary hoo-ha spoils retired friend taking home a trophy

indicators.note: something retired has gone back, so the word for spoils is read from end to start
taking means swallowing up, so the friend word goes around the word for home

blocks.note: spoils as a verb: goes bad, rots
a mate is a friend
at home means in
taken as written
a cup is a sporting trophy

explanation.surface: A sour remark about a pensioner who has carried off a trophy, dismissed as fuss over nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retired' reads as a pensioner's status in the surface, but it turns only the spoils word around; the home word then sits inside the friend.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a great commotion over something trivial, which is exactly needless fuss.

clue.text: Long tale has Scooby Doo, say, following master to gold hidden in farm building

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the dog word is placed behind the master word
something hidden in a place is placed within it, so the gold word goes inside the building word

blocks.note: in the cartoon, Shaggy is Scooby-Doo's owner, his master
Scooby-Doo is an example of a dog; 'say' marks the example
a sty is a pigs' building on a farm
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A summary of a cartoon episode in which Scooby-Doo trails Shaggy towards buried gold in a barn.
explanation.walkthrough: Scooby-Doo's owner in the cartoon is called Shaggy, which is why master gives that name here.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaggy-dog story is a rambling anecdote with a pointless punchline, a long-winded yarn.

clue.text: Jockey used to collect old caps

indicators.note: to jockey is to manoeuvre and jostle about, so these letters are moved into a new order
to collect is to gather in, so the following letter is taken inside

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A rider who once gathered old hats or cricket caps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jockey' looks like the rider in the scene but is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To cap something is to top or better it, which is what one who outdoes another achieves.

clue.text: Very important manuscript holds warning to university

indicators.note: to hold is to keep within, so the manuscript abbreviation wraps around what follows

blocks.note: MS is the standard abbreviation for manuscript
an omen is a warning sign
taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A crucial document containing a caution addressed to a university.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything after 'holds' goes between the two letters of the manuscript abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something momentous is of great consequence, a near synonym for being highly significant.

clue.text: Can't be famous

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: unable to do something
second meaning: well known, worth noticing

explanation.surface: A short lament that one can never achieve fame.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer says 'unable'; read as one word, it means well known. 'Be' just joins the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable person is well known and worthy of attention, a synonym for famous.

clue.text: Feisty fashion model's brought in to give evidence

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the letters are formed into something new
something brought in is added inside, so the model's letter joins the fodder

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
the Model T was Ford's famous car

explanation.surface: A spirited catwalk model is called in as a witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fashion model' reads as one phrase from the catwalk, but fashion is the anagram signal and model is just T.
explanation.definitionFit: To testify is to make a statement as a witness, giving evidence in court.

clue.text: Stuck up a fine outside toilet

indicators.note: outside here means placed beyond the end, so the fine letter stands after the toilet

blocks.note: taken as written
loo is a British word for toilet
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Someone stuck high on an outdoor lavatory roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuck up' sounds physical, as if something is lodged up on the toilet, but it is the definition: snooty.
explanation.definitionFit: Being aloof means keeping a cool distance from others, which reads as haughty or snobbish.

clue.text: Argued about small change in improved software

indicators.note: about suggests turning round or moving around, so the letters get rearranged
in places the small change letter inside the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
P is a penny, the smallest coin

explanation.surface: A row over a minor tweak in a new version of a program.
explanation.definitionFit: An upgrade is a newer, better version of software that replaces the old one.

clue.text: They hold dialogue with company taking millions as net drive development goes ahead

indicators.note: development turns something into a new form, so the two words before it are rearranged
going ahead means moving to the front, so this part is placed first

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
CO is the abbreviation for company
M is million; plural gives two of them
taken as written

explanation.surface: Business jargon about a firm earning millions as an internet project pushes forward.
explanation.definitionFit: Inverted commas are quotation marks, which enclose the spoken words of a conversation in writing.

clue.text: Heartless deed to entice with crack

indicators.note: without a heart, the word loses its central letter

blocks.note: an act is a deed
to tempt is to entice

explanation.surface: A cruel act meant to lure someone with drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like the drug the deed uses as bait; it is the definition, as in 'have a crack at'.
explanation.definitionFit: A crack at something is an informal word for a go or try, an attempt.

clue.text: Having eaten nothing, Nigel's knocked head over heels by home-made liqueur

indicators.note: having eaten something means holding it inside, so the nothing letter is enclosed
knocked head over heels means turned upside down, so in this across entry the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Nigel, drinking on an empty stomach, is floored by a homemade spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloe gin is made by steeping sloes in gin, a liqueur traditionally prepared at home.

clue.text: Utter stress of putting grand on horse

indicators.note: putting one thing on another stacks them, the grand ahead of the horse

blocks.note: G is short for a grand, a thousand pounds
a roan is a horse with a mixed-colour coat

explanation.surface: The sheer anxiety of betting a thousand pounds on a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' looks like an adjective (complete stress) but is the verb: to voice.
explanation.definitionFit: To groan is to give a low sound expressing pain or distress, voicing the strain one feels.

clue.text: Bring up to date on investigation into document carrier

blocks.note: to brief someone is to give them the latest information
a case is a police investigation

explanation.surface: Updating someone on an inquiry about a container for papers.
explanation.definitionFit: A briefcase is a flat bag used to carry papers and documents.

clue.text: Find it's light after the party?

blocks.note: a disco is a dance party
a Very light is a coloured signal flare fired from a pistol

explanation.surface: Someone surprised to find it already daylight when the party ends.
explanation.walkthrough: A Very light is a signal flare named after its inventor; the question mark flags this playful use.
explanation.definitionFit: A discovery is something found, so as a noun it is a find.

clue.text: Put opener on short leg at crease

indicators.note: an opener is what comes first, so only the start of the word is used
short means cut off, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: first letter of the word
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Cricket instructions: send in the opening batsman with a fielder at short leg, at the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: Opener, short leg and crease are all cricket terms, but crease here is a fold in fabric. Short leg is a fielding position close to the batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleat is a fold pressed into cloth, a deliberate crease.

clue.text: For beating a pinata go to part of South America

indicators.note: a beating knocks things about, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Travel to South America for a party where you smash a piñata.
explanation.definitionFit: Patagonia is the region at the southern tip of the continent, shared by Argentina and Chile.

clue.text: Mocks soldiers having to live in

indicators.note: having something in means holding it inside, so the soldiers wrap around the verb

blocks.note: GIs are American soldiers
to be is to exist, to live

explanation.surface: Soldiers taunted for being made to live in barracks.
explanation.definitionFit: To gibe is to taunt or jeer, so gibes is a synonym for mocks.

clue.text: Old boy's upset by seedy part of city

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so in this down entry the letters are read upwards

blocks.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
a rough area is seedy and run-down

explanation.surface: A former pupil distressed by a run-down district.
explanation.definitionFit: A borough is an administrative district, especially within London.

clue.text: Couple of pints before getting daughter installed in digs

blocks.note: a quart is two pints
ere is an old word for before
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A drink or two before settling one's daughter into student lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: Digs is British slang for rented lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: To be quartered is to be lodged or billeted, given accommodation.

clue.text: Nit-picking question about Bible

indicators.note: about suggests the letters are turned around into a new order

blocks.note: qu. is the abbreviation for question
taken as written, as anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A pedantic query about a detail of scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: A quibble is a petty objection, so it names nit-picking as a noun.

clue.text: Colluded with a boy about wager

blocks.note: taken as written
a bet is a wager
Ted is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Someone who conspired with a lad over a bet.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'a boy about wager', but the boy comes last: A, BET, TED; 'about' is loose here.
explanation.definitionFit: To abet is to assist in wrongdoing, so abetted means colluded with.

clue.text: Erupt again about doctor not working

indicators.note: not working means without the little word for working or switched on, so it is removed

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
a surgeon is a kind of doctor

explanation.surface: A doctor is idle, and something is flaring up again.
explanation.walkthrough: ON means working, as a machine is on; drop it from SURGEON.
explanation.definitionFit: To resurge is to rise up again, like a volcano or a conflict breaking out a second time.

clue.text: Bully of a fly half grabs one after blunder

indicators.note: half means only one of the two equal parts of the word is kept
to grab is to seize and hold, so the fly letters wrap around the rest

blocks.note: the tsetse is an African fly
an error is a blunder
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A rugby fly-half who catches someone out after a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly half' looks like the rugby position, but it means half the letters of an African fly's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To terrorise is to frighten and intimidate, which is what bullying does.

clue.text: Legally grown ordinary cigarette's drug, too!

blocks.note: O is an abbreviation for ordinary
fag is British slang for a cigarette
E is slang for ecstasy

explanation.surface: A teenager complaining that a regular smoke counts as a drug too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Legally grown' tempts toward cannabis farming; it means adult in law.
explanation.definitionFit: Being of age means having reached the age of legal adulthood.

clue.text: CGI's more than some gadget

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the words, so a run of letters is taken from inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A claim that computer-generated imagery outshines any mere device.
explanation.definitionFit: A gismo, also spelt gizmo, is an informal word for a gadget or device.

clue.text: Plant is focal point in river bar refurbishment

indicators.note: in places the focal point inside the other letters
a refurbishment rebuilds and rearranges, so the letters before it are reordered

blocks.note: a hub is a centre of activity
R is short for river, and bar is taken as written

explanation.surface: A greenery feature as centrepiece of a riverside pub makeover.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhubarb is a plant whose pink stalks are cooked as a dessert ingredient.

clue.text: Paddy volunteers to swap funny books

indicators.note: swapping changes the order of the two words that follow, so the second comes first

blocks.note: the TA was the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve
NT is the New Testament, a set of books
rum is British informal for odd or funny

explanation.surface: Paddy and some volunteers trading comic books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like a person's name; in British slang a paddy is a fit of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A tantrum is an outburst of bad temper, the same thing as a paddy.

clue.text: Wide boys were held improperly by auditors getting to grips with large earnings, initially

indicators.note: improperly means not in the right way, so the letters are put out of order
initially points to the first letters of the words just before it
grasping something means holding it, so the listeners enclose the letters

blocks.note: taken as written, as anagram fodder
auditors are listeners, and ears do the listening
first letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Spivs kept under suspicion by accountants scrutinising big profits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditors' suggests accountants checking the books; it means listeners. A wide boy is British slang for a shady operator.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheeler-dealers are shrewd, often dodgy traders, just like wide boys who live by their wits.
